database_metadata.name: AI-Driven Cyber Attack Progression Prediction System - Zeek-to-MITRE ATT&CK Mapping Database
database_metadata.description: Machine-readable Zeek telemetry to MITRE ATT&CK technique mapping database with structured correlation rules for behavioral detection.
schema_notes: All correlation rules are declarative, machine-readable, and SQL-free.
The generic correlation engine consumes correlation_rule fields directly.
Field names preserve original Zeek log field naming (conn.id.orig_h, etc.).
Endpoint confirmation is represented via external_context, not fabricated fields.
confidence_score represents mapping strength, not runtime detection confidence.

evidence_conditions: Single source IP (id.orig_h) initiates connections to multiple distinct destination ports (id.resp_p)
Connection states predominantly S0 (connection attempt seen, no reply) or REJ (connection attempt rejected)
High frequency of connections within short time window
Target hosts may be sequential or within same subnet
Connection duration is very short (scanning behavior)
mappings.false_positive_notes: Network vulnerability scanners (Nessus, OpenVAS), legitimate asset discovery tools, and automated monitoring systems may trigger this. Verify against known scanner IPs and scan schedules.
mappings.explanation: Port scanning produces distinctive patterns in conn.log: a single host rapidly probes multiple ports across one or more targets. Zeek captures each connection attempt with conn_state reflecting the scan type (S0 for SYN scans, REJ for connect scans). The behavioral correlation engine must aggregate by source IP and count unique destination ports within a time window to distinguish scanning from normal traffic.

evidence_conditions: Single source IP targets single destination IP on many ports
Sequential port numbers or common service ports targeted
Connection states S0 or REJ dominant
Very short connection durations
mappings.false_positive_notes: Application health checks, load balancer probes, and some monitoring tools perform multi-port checks. Cross-reference with asset inventory.
mappings.explanation: Vertical scanning targets a single host across many ports. In conn.log, this appears as numerous conn records sharing the same orig_h and resp_h but varying resp_p. The correlation engine groups by source-target pair and counts unique ports.

evidence_conditions: Single source IP connects to sequential or numerous IPs within same subnet/CIDR block
Same destination port across all connections
Connection states predominantly S0 or REJ
High connection rate spanning subnet range
mappings.false_positive_notes: Network discovery protocols and broadcast traffic may appear similar. This lab does not use DHCP, reducing false positives.
mappings.explanation: IP block scanning targets an entire subnet rather than individual hosts. In conn.log, this manifests as a single source connecting to many hosts within the same /24 or larger prefix, typically on the same port. The correlation engine must identify subnet-level targeting patterns.

evidence_conditions: Single source IP makes many HTTP requests to same host with varied URIs
High ratio of 404 Not Found or 400 Bad Request responses
URIs contain known vulnerability patterns: SQL injection probes, path traversal attempts, common exploit paths
User-Agent may reveal scanner identity (Nikto, Nessus, OpenVAS, sqlmap)
Rapid request rate exceeding normal browsing behavior
mappings.false_positive_notes: Web crawlers (Googlebot), security assessment tools run by administrators, and broken link checkers may trigger. Validate against scheduled scanning activities and user agent strings.
mappings.explanation: Web vulnerability scanners generate highly distinctive http.log patterns: rapid-fire requests to numerous URLs on a target host, with most returning 404/400 errors as the scanner probes for vulnerable endpoints. The correlation engine must count unique URIs, measure error ratios, and detect scanner user-agents or malicious URI patterns.

evidence_conditions: Single source IP queries many hostnames within target domain
Sequential subdomain enumeration (e.g., admin, www, mail, ftp, dev, test)
A/AAAA queries for hosts that do not exist (rcode = NXDOMAIN)
High query rate exceeding normal DNS client behavior

supporting_conditions.description: Queries share same domain suffix (subdomain enumeration)

mappings.false_positive_notes: Web browsers with prefetching, anti-virus software, and some applications perform multiple DNS lookups. However, subdomain enumeration patterns (dictionary words, sequential) are distinct.
mappings.explanation: DNS-based reconnaissance involves enumerating subdomains to map target infrastructure. In dns.log, this appears as numerous A/AAAA queries from a single source for varying subdomains of the same domain, often with NXDOMAIN responses for non-existent hosts. The correlation engine groups by source IP and detects enumeration patterns.

evidence_conditions: Connection to multiple internal hosts on banner-grabbing ports
Ports: 21 (FTP), 23 (Telnet), 25 (SMTP), 110 (POP3), 143 (IMAP), 3306 (MySQL), 5432 (PostgreSQL)
Connection state S0 or REJ (port probing)
Very short duration (<1 second)
Pattern suggests service version enumeration
mappings.false_positive_notes: Network inventory tools and some monitoring systems perform service enumeration. Distinguished by source host role and scan pattern.
mappings.explanation: Host information gathering involves identifying services and versions running on target systems. In conn.log, this appears as connections to banner-grabbing ports across multiple hosts with very short durations. The correlation engine detects service enumeration patterns.

evidence_conditions: Single source IP requests many different paths/URIs on same web server
High ratio of 404 Not Found responses indicates path guessing
URIs contain common directory names: /admin, /backup, /config, /.env, /phpmyadmin
URIs may contain path traversal patterns: ../../, ..%2f, %2e%2e%2f
Request rate exceeds normal browsing (no referrer, no linked page structure)
mappings.false_positive_notes: Broken link checkers, some web crawlers, and misconfigured applications may generate 404s. However, directory enumeration patterns and lack of referrer information distinguish malicious scanning.
mappings.explanation: Web directory enumeration is a form of file and directory discovery. In http.log, attackers probe for sensitive directories and files by requesting common paths. The correlation engine identifies this by counting unique URIs with high 404 ratios from a single source, especially when paths match known sensitive directories.

evidence_conditions: Single source IP connects to multiple internal hosts on same port
Common ports: 445 (SMB), 3389 (RDP), 22 (SSH), 5985 (WinRM), 80/443 (HTTP)
Connection state S0 indicates host may be offline or port closed
SF or S1 states indicate successful connection to live host
Pattern suggests systematic host enumeration

supporting_conditions.description: Connection state distribution shows mix of S0 (offline) and SF/S1 (live)

mappings.false_positive_notes: Network management tools, inventory scanners, and legitimate administration scripts may connect to many hosts. Context of source IP (admin workstation vs. compromised host) is critical.
mappings.explanation: Remote system discovery involves identifying live hosts on the network. In conn.log, this appears as connections from a single source to many destination IPs, typically on common service ports. Live hosts return SF/S1 states while offline hosts return S0. The correlation engine counts unique destination hosts per source and port.

evidence_conditions: Single source IP establishes connections to many internal hosts across varied ports
Connections followed by quick termination after minimal data exchange
Pattern suggests mapping active services rather than exploiting them
May combine with DNS queries for discovered hosts
mappings.false_positive_notes: Network monitoring systems, discovery protocols, and some legitimate applications connect broadly. Low data transfer volume helps distinguish reconnaissance from legitimate use.
mappings.explanation: Network connections discovery maps active services and hosts. In conn.log, this appears as a single source connecting to many hosts and ports with minimal data transfer, suggesting service enumeration rather than exploitation. The correlation engine groups by source and looks for breadth of connections with low byte counts.

evidence_conditions: Repeated HTTP POST/GET requests to same unusual URI (e.g., /uploads/shell.jsp, /images/config.php)
URI contains command-like parameters: ?cmd=, ?exec=, ?command=, ?run=, /bin/sh
Requests lack referrer and have minimal or attacker-specific User-Agent
Response body contains command output patterns: directory listings, system information, error messages
Request and response body sizes inconsistent with normal web page traffic
Activity occurs outside business hours or from unusual source IPs

supporting_conditions.description: Referrer is NULL or User-Agent is suspicious
Correlation with files.log showing script mime_type on same URI

mappings.false_positive_notes: Legitimate API endpoints, administrative interfaces, and some web applications use command-like parameters. Web shells are distinguished by unusual URI paths, lack of referrer, and command-output responses.
mappings.explanation: Active web shell usage produces behavioral patterns in http.log: repeated requests to an unusual URI with command parameters, minimal headers, and responses containing system command output. The correlation engine must identify persistent access to non-standard URIs with command-like request patterns.

evidence_conditions: Internal host initiates SMB connection to another internal host
Destination port 445 is used
Source host communicates with multiple SMB targets in a short period
Large SMB transfers occur after authentication events
Behavior differs from normal baseline activity

supporting_conditions.description: Followed by authentication activity or remote execution telemetry

mappings.false_positive_notes: File servers, backup systems, domain controllers, and administrative tools commonly generate SMB traffic. Baseline normal SMB behavior before alerting.
mappings.explanation: Zeek can observe SMB network communication and lateral movement patterns but cannot determine whether credential dumping occurred. Credential access techniques require endpoint telemetry such as Sysmon process access events or Windows security auditing.

evidence_conditions: Multiple SSH connection attempts from same source IP to same destination IP
auth_success = F (false) for majority of attempts
High frequency of attempts within short time window
May see varying client versions or consistent attacker tool signature
Connection duration is very short (failed authentication)
mappings.false_positive_notes: Automated scripts with wrong credentials, misconfigured applications, and legitimate users with expired passwords. Distinguished by high volume and consistent failure pattern.
mappings.explanation: SSH brute force attacks produce clear patterns in ssh.log: numerous connection attempts from one source to one target with auth_success consistently false. Zeek captures each SSH authentication attempt. The correlation engine groups by source-target pair and counts failed attempts within a time window.

evidence_conditions: Multiple HTTP POST requests to login/authentication endpoint from same source
URI contains login paths: /login, /auth, /signin, /wp-login.php, /administrator
Status code patterns: 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, or 200 with redirect to login
Request body length consistent with username/password submission
User-Agent may be missing, generic, or automation tool signature
High frequency of attempts within short window

supporting_conditions.description: Request body length consistent with credential submission

mappings.false_positive_notes: Legitimate users with forgotten passwords, automated monitoring systems testing authentication, and some mobile applications. Distinguished by volume and failure patterns.
mappings.explanation: HTTP-based brute force attacks target web application login forms. In http.log, this appears as repeated POST requests to authentication endpoints with failure status codes. Zeek captures the method, URI, status code, and timing. The correlation engine groups by source and login endpoint to detect brute force patterns.

evidence_conditions: Many SSH authentication attempts from single source to single target
auth_success = F for all or most attempts
Attempts use same username with varying passwords (inferred from rapid retry pattern)
Time between attempts is consistent with automated password guessing
Eventually may succeed (auth_success = T) indicating password cracked

supporting_conditions.description: Followed by successful authentication within 300 seconds

mappings.false_positive_notes: Legitimate users with password issues, automated backup scripts with stale credentials. Distinguished by volume and automation patterns.
mappings.explanation: Password guessing focuses on a single account with many password attempts. In ssh.log, this appears as repeated failed authentications from one source to one target in rapid succession. Zeek does not capture the actual password, but the volume and timing pattern indicate password guessing.

evidence_conditions: Single source IP attempts SSH to multiple destination IPs
Few attempts per target (typically 1-3) to avoid lockout
auth_success may be F or T
Same password likely used across targets (inferred from timing and pattern)
Low and slow pattern: attempts spaced to evade detection
mappings.false_positive_notes: Configuration management tools (Ansible, Puppet) and legitimate administrative scripts may SSH to many hosts. Distinguished by authentication success rate and source IP context.
mappings.explanation: Password spraying uses one password against many accounts to avoid lockout thresholds. In ssh.log, this appears as a single source connecting to many targets with very few attempts per target. The correlation engine must detect the breadth-over-depth pattern that distinguishes spraying from targeted brute force.

evidence_conditions: Single source IP sends login requests to multiple different hosts or user endpoints
Few attempts per target (1-3) to avoid account lockout
Same login URI pattern across targets
Status codes indicate authentication failures
Timing is distributed to evade rate limiting
mappings.false_positive_notes: Single sign-on systems, federation services, and legitimate multi-system authentication. Context of source IP and authentication infrastructure is important.
mappings.explanation: HTTP password spraying targets multiple web applications or user accounts with few attempts each. In http.log, this appears as login requests to many hosts from one source with minimal attempts per target. The correlation engine detects the distributed attack pattern across multiple targets.

evidence_conditions: Single internal source connects to multiple internal targets on port 22
Connection states SF or S1 indicating successful SSH sessions
Duration > 30 seconds per connection
Sequential connections suggest automated lateral movement
Source host accessed targets in rapid succession

supporting_conditions.description: Correlation with ssh.log auth_success = T for these connections

mappings.false_positive_notes: Ansible playbooks, configuration management, and administrative scripts may SSH to many hosts. Distinguished by timing regularity and host role context.
mappings.explanation: SSH lateral movement across multiple targets produces a distinctive conn.log pattern: one source connecting to many internal targets on port 22 with successful connection states. The correlation engine groups by source and counts unique targets to detect lateral movement patterns.

evidence_conditions: Connection to internal service port followed by unusual protocol behavior
Connection state S0 or REJ may indicate exploit attempt against closed/filtered port
Connection with SF state but service field mismatch (e.g., HTTP traffic on SMB port)
Rapid connection to same port across many internal hosts (exploit sweep)
Large unexpected data transfer following connection to service port

supporting_conditions.description: Service mismatch or unusual byte pattern
Correlation with weird.log or notice.log for same connections

mappings.false_positive_notes: Port forwarding, NAT traversal, and some legitimate services may use non-standard ports. Service mismatch alone is not sufficient without additional exploit indicators.
mappings.explanation: Remote service exploitation for lateral movement may produce network indicators in conn.log: exploit sweeps across internal hosts, service mismatches, or unusual data patterns following connection establishment. This is a behavioral mapping because exploitation is primarily an endpoint activity; network indicators are secondary.

evidence_conditions: Regular HTTP requests from internal host to external host at consistent intervals (beaconing)
URI paths are unusual: random strings, encoded data, or consistent pattern (e.g., /news/abc123, /update/xyz789)
User-Agent is generic, missing, or matches known malware families
Request and response body lengths are consistent (command/request sizes, response/data sizes)
No referrer header on any request
Requests occur outside business hours or during system idle times
Host header may be IP address rather than domain name

supporting_conditions.description: URI contains encoded data or random strings

mappings.false_positive_notes: Software update checks, cloud synchronization clients, and some monitoring agents exhibit regular HTTP patterns. Distinguished by domain reputation, URI structure, and user agent analysis.
mappings.explanation: HTTP-based C2 channels produce beaconing patterns in http.log: regular requests to external hosts with consistent timing, unusual URIs, and minimal headers. The correlation engine must analyze inter-request intervals for consistency (low coefficient of variation), detect missing referrers, and identify suspicious URI patterns.

evidence_conditions: Regular TLS connections from internal host to external host at consistent intervals
SNI (server_name) may be missing, IP-based, or use suspicious domains
Certificate subject/issuer may be self-signed, suspicious, or match known malicious indicators
Validation status may indicate certificate issues (unable to verify, self-signed)
Cipher suite may be weak or unusual
Connection duration and byte transfer show periodic data exchange pattern

supporting_conditions.description: Certificate is self-signed or has suspicious issuer

mappings.false_positive_notes: Cloud services, CDN connections, and legitimate HTTPS APIs may show regular patterns. Distinguished by certificate validity, domain reputation, and SNI analysis.
mappings.explanation: HTTPS C2 channels encrypt traffic but still produce observable patterns in ssl.log and conn.log. Zeek captures TLS handshake metadata including SNI, certificate details, and cipher suites. Beaconing patterns in SSL connections with certificate anomalies provide strong behavioral evidence of C2 communication.

evidence_conditions: Regular DNS queries from internal host to external DNS server at consistent intervals
Query names are suspicious: DGA-like (random characters), very long subdomains, or encoded data
Query type consistently A or AAAA (tunneling often uses A records for response data)
Response answers contain unusual IP addresses or patterns
High volume of queries to same domain with varying subdomains
Queries to domains with short TTLs or recently registered domains

supporting_conditions.description: Domain has short TTL or recently registered

mappings.false_positive_notes: CDN load balancing, anti-virus cloud lookups, and some legitimate applications use multiple subdomains. DGA detection and query entropy analysis help distinguish C2 from legitimate traffic.
mappings.explanation: DNS-based C2 uses DNS queries and responses to tunnel commands and data. In dns.log, this appears as regular queries with unusual subdomain patterns, high entropy names, or encoded data. The correlation engine must detect beaconing intervals, DGA patterns, and high query volumes to the same domain with varying subdomains.

evidence_conditions: Extremely high volume of DNS queries from single internal host
Query names are very long (>60 characters) with encoded or random subdomains
Query types alternate between A and TXT (common tunneling pattern)
Response answers contain base64-like or hex-encoded data
Queries to single domain with hundreds of unique subdomains
Query rate far exceeds normal DNS client behavior (>1 query per second sustained)

supporting_conditions.description: Response answers contain base64-like or hex-encoded data

mappings.false_positive_notes: Some CDN and cloud services generate many DNS queries. However, extremely long queries and TXT record tunneling are rare in legitimate traffic. Query length and rate are strong discriminators.
mappings.explanation: DNS tunneling encapsulates non-DNS protocol data within DNS queries and responses. Zeek dns.log captures query names, types, and answers. Tunneling produces distinctive patterns: very long queries with encoded data, high query rates, and TXT record usage. The correlation engine must analyze query length distribution, rate, and record type patterns.

evidence_conditions: Sustained TCP or UDP connection to external host with no recognized application protocol
Service field is empty or '-' indicating unknown protocol
Regular byte transfer in both directions suggesting active communication
Connection duration is long (>300 seconds) with periodic data exchange
Port number is unusual and not associated with known services
mappings.false_positive_notes: Custom applications, gaming traffic, and some VPN protocols may use raw TCP/UDP. Distinguished by destination reputation, port analysis, and connection patterns.
mappings.explanation: Raw TCP/UDP C2 channels avoid application-layer detection by using custom protocols. Zeek conn.log captures these as connections with empty service fields and sustained data transfer. The correlation engine must detect persistent connections with regular data exchange on unrecognized protocols.

evidence_conditions: Sustained connection to known C2 destination (correlated with T1071 mapping)
Periodic large data transfers from internal to external host
orig_bytes significantly larger than resp_bytes (data upload pattern)
Transfer occurs during established C2 session
Data transfer rate is consistent with automated exfiltration
Connection shows beaconing pattern followed by large burst transfer

supporting_conditions.description: Prior T1071 mapping for same orig_h, resp_h pair

mappings.false_positive_notes: Cloud backups, file synchronization services, and legitimate large uploads may appear similar. Correlation with C2 beaconing is essential for distinguishing exfiltration from legitimate activity.
mappings.explanation: Exfiltration over C2 channels uses the existing command and control connection to transfer data. In conn.log, this appears as large data transfers from internal to external hosts during established C2 sessions. The correlation engine must link the data transfer to a previously identified C2 channel and analyze byte ratios to distinguish exfiltration from normal C2 traffic.

evidence_conditions: Large HTTP POST requests from internal host to external host
POST body size is unusually large (>1MB) for typical web requests
URI may be unusual or appear to be a data dump endpoint
User-Agent is generic, missing, or does not match known applications
No prior browsing activity to same host (no GET requests, no referrer)
Request occurs outside business hours or after suspicious activity

supporting_conditions.description: Referrer is NULL or User-Agent is suspicious

mappings.false_positive_notes: Cloud storage uploads, file sharing services, and legitimate API bulk uploads. Distinguished by host reputation, URI patterns, and user agent analysis.
mappings.explanation: HTTP exfiltration uploads data to external servers via large POST requests. In http.log, this appears as unusually large request bodies to external hosts without normal browsing context. The correlation engine must detect large POST volumes and distinguish them from legitimate uploads.

evidence_conditions: Extremely high volume of DNS queries from single internal host
Query names contain encoded data (base64, hex) in subdomains
Query length is very long (>70 characters) suggesting data encoding
Query rate exceeds 1 per second sustained over minutes
Queries to single domain with unique subdomains (data chunks)
TXT or NULL record queries used for larger data transfer
mappings.false_positive_notes: Very rare in legitimate traffic. Some security tools and DNS-based services generate queries but not at exfiltration volumes. Query length and rate are strong discriminators.
mappings.explanation: DNS tunneling for exfiltration encodes data in query names and sends it to attacker-controlled DNS servers. Zeek dns.log captures every query. Exfiltration produces higher volumes and longer queries than C2 tunneling because data must be chunked and transmitted. The correlation engine must detect sustained high-rate querying with very long encoded subdomains.

evidence_conditions: Large HTTP POST/PUT requests to known cloud storage or web service domains
Target domains: dropbox.com, drive.google.com, pastebin.com, github.com, mega.nz, etc.
Request body size is large (>5MB) suggesting file upload
User-Agent may be API client or generic HTTP client
Activity occurs after suspicious endpoint activity or during off-hours
No prior normal browsing pattern to same service

supporting_conditions.description: Prior T1071 or T1190 on same orig_h

mappings.false_positive_notes: Legitimate cloud backup services, file synchronization, and developer uploads. Distinguished by account ownership, upload timing, and correlation with suspicious activity.
mappings.explanation: Exfiltration over web services uses legitimate cloud platforms to avoid detection. In http.log, this appears as large uploads to known cloud storage domains. The correlation engine must detect large POST/PUT requests to cloud services and correlate with prior suspicious activity to distinguish malicious exfiltration from legitimate use.

evidence_conditions: Large outbound data transfer to external host on unusual port
orig_bytes > 50MB with minimal resp_bytes
Port is not associated with known legitimate service for source host
Connection is sustained and shows consistent upload rate
Destination IP may be in suspicious geographic location or have poor reputation

supporting_conditions.description: resp_p not in known legitimate ports

mappings.false_positive_notes: Legitimate large uploads, cloud backups, and data synchronization. Distinguished by destination reputation, port analysis, and host role context.
mappings.explanation: Alternative protocol exfiltration uses non-standard protocols or ports to transfer data. Zeek conn.log captures all connections regardless of port. Large outbound transfers on unusual ports with minimal return traffic provide behavioral evidence of exfiltration.

evidence_conditions: Connection to port 445 (SMB) from internal host to file server
Large data transfer (resp_bytes >> orig_bytes) indicating file download
Sustained connection duration (>120 seconds) suggesting bulk file access
Source host is not typical user of target file server
Connection occurs after lateral movement or compromise indicators

supporting_conditions.description: Correlation with T1021.002 (SMB lateral movement) on same orig_h within 300 seconds

mappings.false_positive_notes: Legitimate file server access, backup operations, and administrative file copies. This is a weak indicator without endpoint correlation.
mappings.explanation: Data collection from network shares may produce SMB connection patterns in conn.log: large downloads from file servers. Zeek does not parse SMB file operations in standard configurations, so this mapping relies on connection metadata. The correlation engine must link large SMB transfers to lateral movement indicators for meaningful detection.

evidence_conditions: HTTP requests to internal web application database endpoints or API resources
URI contains database-related paths: /api/data, /export, /download, /backup, /dump
Large response body sizes indicating bulk data retrieval
Requests from unusual source IPs or after compromise indicators
Method may be GET or POST with query parameters targeting data export

supporting_conditions.description: Prior T1190 or T1071 on same orig_h

mappings.false_positive_notes: Legitimate data exports, backups, and administrative downloads. Context of source host and timing is critical.
mappings.explanation: Data collection from web-based information repositories may appear in http.log as large downloads from application APIs or export endpoints. Zeek captures request and response sizes. The correlation engine must detect bulk data retrieval patterns and link them to compromise indicators.

attack_technique.technique_name: Application Layer Protocol: File Transfer Protocols

evidence_conditions: FTP connection from internal host to external FTP server
Regular connection pattern suggesting C2 channel over FTP
Commands include STOR/RETR with small files (command/data exchange)
Connection occurs at consistent intervals
User credentials may be generic or suspicious

supporting_conditions.description: Commands include STOR/RETR with small file sizes

mappings.false_positive_notes: Legacy systems, some backup solutions, and specific industry applications still use FTP. Evaluate against known business requirements.
mappings.explanation: FTP may be used as a C2 channel in environments where HTTP/HTTPS is heavily monitored. Zeek ftp.log captures FTP session commands. Regular FTP connections to external servers with small file transfers may indicate C2 communication.

evidence_conditions: Connection to multiple internal hosts on banner-grabbing ports
Ports: 21 (FTP), 23 (Telnet), 25 (SMTP), 110 (POP3), 143 (IMAP), 3306 (MySQL), 5432 (PostgreSQL)
Connection state S0 or REJ (port probing)
Very short duration (<1 second)
Pattern suggests service version enumeration
mappings.false_positive_notes: Network inventory tools and some monitoring systems perform service enumeration. Distinguished by source host role and scan pattern.
mappings.explanation: Host information gathering involves identifying services and versions running on target systems. In conn.log, this appears as connections to banner-grabbing ports across multiple hosts with very short durations. The correlation engine detects service enumeration patterns.

evidence_conditions: Sustained TCP connections to known mining pool IPs/domains
Connection duration is very long (>1 hour) with regular small data exchange
orig_bytes and resp_bytes show consistent small packet sizes (share submissions)
Multiple connections from same host to different mining pools

supporting_conditions.description: resp_h matches known mining pool IOCs

mappings.false_positive_notes: Some legitimate applications use similar ports. Mining pool IP/domain reputation is the strongest discriminator.
mappings.explanation: Cryptomining resource hijacking produces distinctive network patterns: long-duration connections to mining pools on specific ports with regular small data exchanges. Zeek conn.log captures these persistent connections. The correlation engine must detect connections to known mining infrastructure.

evidence_conditions: DNS queries for sandbox/analysis environment indicators
Query names contain sandbox vendor domains: virustotal.com, joesecurity.org, any.run
Queries for time servers followed by geographic location checks
Pattern suggests malware checking if running in analysis environment
mappings.false_positive_notes: Security researchers and administrators may query sandbox services. Low confidence reflects indirect evidence.
mappings.explanation: Malware may check for sandbox environments by querying known analysis services or performing time/location checks. Zeek dns.log can capture these queries. This is indirect evidence requiring correlation with endpoint behavior.

evidence_conditions: Single internal host generates queries for many unique domains within short time window
Queried domains contain high entropy subdomains or randomly generated structures
High ratio of failed DNS resolutions (NXDOMAIN responses)
Domain length and character distribution show algorithmic generation patterns
Repeated DNS queries indicate automated C2 resolution attempts

supporting_conditions.description: Query intervals show periodic beaconing behavior

mappings.false_positive_notes: CDN providers and cloud services may generate random-looking hostnames. Domain reputation enrichment and known-good domain filtering are required.
mappings.explanation: DGA malware generates large numbers of pseudo-random domains to locate C2 infrastructure. Zeek dns.log provides visibility into query volume, entropy, and DNS response behavior. Correlation between these features provides probabilistic detection.

evidence_conditions: Single internal host generates excessive DNS queries to one external domain
Query names contain encoded data patterns such as Base64 or hexadecimal strings
DNS query length is unusually large
Subdomains follow sequential chunking patterns
High query frequency maintained over time
mappings.false_positive_notes: SPF, DKIM, and legitimate TXT queries may create abnormal DNS patterns. Encoding detection and query frequency are required.
mappings.explanation: DNS tunneling and DNS-based exfiltration encode data inside DNS queries. Zeek can detect abnormal query size, frequency, and encoding characteristics.

evidence_conditions: Browser-like HTTP traffic from internal host to suspicious external domain
HTTP response delivers executable, script, or suspicious document file
Downloaded file has uncommon extension or suspicious MIME type
Domain reputation indicates malicious infrastructure
mappings.false_positive_notes: Software updates and legitimate downloads may create similar behavior.
mappings.explanation: Zeek cannot confirm browser exploitation, but it can detect suspicious browsing followed by potentially malicious file delivery. Endpoint telemetry is required for confirmation.

evidence_conditions: Periodic DNS queries from one internal host to external domains
Consistent beacon interval with timing variation
Domains show high entropy or suspicious reputation
Resolved IP addresses change frequently
mappings.false_positive_notes: CDN traffic and cloud applications may generate periodic DNS queries.
mappings.explanation: DNS is frequently abused as a C2 channel. Zeek provides query timing, domain behavior, and resolution information required for behavioral detection.

attack_technique.technique_name: Gather Victim Network Information: Domain Properties

evidence_conditions: DNS queries for MX, NS, SOA, or TXT records for a target domain
Queries originate from a non-DNS-server internal host
Multiple record types queried for the same domain in sequence
Queries for subdomains or wildcard patterns
mappings.false_positive_notes: Email servers, mail clients, and legitimate applications query MX records. DNS resolvers query NS records. The role of the originating host is important for distinguishing reconnaissance from legitimate DNS activity.
mappings.explanation: DNS reconnaissance for domain properties involves querying MX, NS, SOA, and TXT records to identify domain infrastructure. Zeek dns.log directly exposes qtype_name, allowing these queries to be detected at the event level.

external_context.notes: Source host location and role require asset inventory or network context. Temporal behavior involving multiple record types requires correlation across DNS events.

evidence_conditions: PTR queries for internal IP ranges
Queries for internal domain names from non-infrastructure hosts
Queries targeting internal DNS or NTP infrastructure
mappings.false_positive_notes: Applications and services commonly perform reverse DNS lookups. Confidence is moderate because a single PTR query is weak evidence without additional context.
mappings.explanation: Network configuration discovery may involve reverse DNS queries used to identify internal hosts and infrastructure. Zeek dns.log captures PTR queries and their target domains.

external_context.notes: Host classification and query target classification require external asset and network context. Internal IP range membership may also require network boundary configuration.

evidence_conditions: Zeek notice generated for a known exploit attempt
Notice indicates HTTP::SQL_Injection, HTTP::Shellshock, HTTP::APTSimulator, or another exploit-related category
Source is external and destination is an internal web server
Notice message contains exploit-specific indicators
mappings.false_positive_notes: Zeek notice detection can produce false positives for complex application behavior. Verification with application and endpoint telemetry is recommended.
mappings.explanation: Exploit-related Zeek notices provide strong network evidence of an attempted exploitation of a public-facing application.

external_context.notes: Source and destination network location require network boundary context. Destination role requires asset inventory.

evidence_conditions: HTTP request contains SQL injection, path traversal, or command injection patterns
Unusual HTTP methods such as PUT, DELETE, or PATCH
Large request body
HTTP 500 response following suspicious request
Suspicious or missing user agent

external_context.notes: Public-facing application classification requires network and asset context. Endpoint classification is not available directly from http.log.

mappings.false_positive_notes: Legitimate APIs, web application testing, search functionality, and content management systems may produce similar patterns.
mappings.explanation: HTTP exploitation attempts can be detected through suspicious URI patterns, HTTP methods, and server error responses. External-to-internal traffic targeting a known web server increases confidence.

evidence_conditions: HTTP protocol anomaly detected
Malformed HTTP request or invalid HTTP verb
Weird event targets a web server port

external_context.notes: Source and destination locations and destination server role require external context.

mappings.false_positive_notes: Broken clients, proxies, and malformed legitimate requests can generate protocol anomalies.
mappings.explanation: Protocol anomalies targeting an internal web server from an external source may indicate exploitation attempts.

evidence_conditions: External source connects to internal host on a remote access port
Remote access ports include SSH, RDP, VNC, and WinRM
Connection is established
Duration exceeds 60 seconds
mappings.false_positive_notes: Legitimate remote administration, VPN access, and third-party support are common.
mappings.explanation: External remote services can provide an initial access path. External-to-internal connections on remote administration ports provide direct network evidence.

external_context.notes: Internal/external classification requires network boundary configuration.

evidence_conditions: Successful SSH authentication
Source is external
Source is not a known VPN or administrative host
Source location is unexpected

external_context.notes: VPN, administrative-host, and geolocation classification require external context. Brute-force history requires temporal correlation.

mappings.false_positive_notes: Remote workers, VPN users, and third-party contractors may legitimately authenticate externally.
mappings.explanation: A successful SSH authentication from an unexpected external source can indicate use of compromised valid credentials.

evidence_conditions: RDP connection from external source to internal host
Connection is established
Duration exceeds 300 seconds
Source is not a known administrative host

external_context.notes: Network boundaries and administrative host classification require external context.

mappings.false_positive_notes: Remote desktop administration and remote workers commonly generate this traffic.
mappings.explanation: A sustained external RDP connection to an internal host may indicate use of valid compromised credentials, although Zeek cannot directly prove successful RDP authentication.

evidence_conditions: HTTP POST or PUT request uploads a file
Uploaded file has a script or executable extension
Upload endpoint is not a known legitimate upload endpoint
Upload succeeds
Filename extension and MIME type are inconsistent
mappings.false_positive_notes: Legitimate CMS uploads, document repositories, and development systems can upload executable-looking files.
mappings.explanation: Uploading a server-side script to a web application can indicate web shell placement. Zeek can observe the HTTP request and transferred file metadata.

external_context.notes: Web-server classification and upload endpoint legitimacy require application and asset inventory context.

evidence_conditions: Internal host downloads an executable, script, archive, or tool
Downloaded file has a suspicious extension
HTTP response is 200
File transfer is confirmed by files.log

external_context.notes: Internal/external network classification requires network boundary context. Execution requires endpoint telemetry and is not inferred from the download alone.

mappings.false_positive_notes: Software updates, package managers, browser downloads, and enterprise deployment systems can produce similar transfers.
mappings.explanation: Zeek can observe file transfers but cannot determine whether the downloaded tool was subsequently executed.

evidence_conditions: Executable file downloaded through HTTP
MIME type indicates executable content
File extension is executable
Destination is an internal workstation

external_context.notes: Destination host classification requires asset inventory. Threat-intelligence hash checking is external enrichment rather than an event-level condition.

mappings.false_positive_notes: Legitimate software downloads, installers, and updates can match these conditions.
mappings.explanation: Executable files transferred to internal workstations can provide evidence of possible client-side exploitation or malware delivery.

evidence_conditions: Browser downloads potentially executable content
Referrer is present
User-Agent indicates browser activity
Downloaded file has an executable or script extension

external_context.notes: Domain reputation requires threat-intelligence or reputation enrichment. Actual user execution cannot be established from Zeek HTTP telemetry alone.

mappings.false_positive_notes: Legitimate downloads and user-initiated file transfers are common.
mappings.explanation: Zeek can observe a suspicious file download that may precede user execution, but cannot directly prove that the user executed the file.

evidence_conditions: HTTP download of command scripts
Download originates from an external server
HTTP response is 200
File metadata confirms script transfer

external_context.notes: Network location classification requires external network context.

mappings.false_positive_notes: Administrative scripts, software deployment systems, and automation frameworks may legitimately transfer scripts.
mappings.explanation: Zeek detects transfer of script files but cannot confirm their execution.

evidence_conditions: RDP connection between internal hosts
Established RDP session
Duration exceeds 60 seconds
Significant bidirectional traffic

external_context.notes: Internal host classification and typical RDP client role require asset inventory.

mappings.false_positive_notes: Legitimate remote administration and help desk activity can produce this pattern.
mappings.explanation: RDP between internal hosts can represent lateral movement. Source and destination host context helps distinguish administrative activity from anomalous movement.

evidence_conditions: SMB connection between internal hosts
Connection is established
Source is a workstation
Source connects to administrative servers

external_context.notes: Host locations and source role require asset inventory. SMB share names require SMB protocol telemetry and are not available from conn.log alone.

mappings.false_positive_notes: Normal file-server access and administrative activity can produce SMB connections.
mappings.explanation: SMB connections on port 445 provide network evidence associated with Windows lateral movement, but conn.log alone cannot prove access to ADMIN$ or C$ shares.

evidence_conditions: Successful SSH authentication between internal hosts
Source host is not a typical SSH client
Source subsequently connects to additional internal hosts

external_context.notes: Host locations and source role require asset inventory. Subsequent connections require temporal correlation.

mappings.false_positive_notes: Legitimate administration, automation, and developer access may generate successful internal SSH sessions.
mappings.explanation: Successful SSH authentication between internal hosts is consistent with lateral movement, especially when the source host is not normally used for SSH administration.

evidence_conditions: Known application protocol detected on an unusual port
HTTP detected outside common HTTP ports
SSH detected outside port 22
DNS detected outside port 53

external_context.notes: Protocol and port mismatch can be evaluated directly from conn.log. Destination reputation or sustained C2 behavior may be added later through enrichment or correlation.

mappings.false_positive_notes: Legitimate services may use non-standard ports.
mappings.explanation: Attackers can use non-standard ports to hide application protocols. Zeek's service identification allows protocol/port mismatches to be detected.

evidence_conditions: HTTP GET downloads an executable or script
HTTP response is 200
Downloaded file is larger than 10 KB
File extension or MIME type indicates executable content

external_context.notes: Network location requires network boundary context. Suspicious activity preceding the transfer requires temporal correlation.

mappings.false_positive_notes: Legitimate software downloads and updates can produce similar traffic.
mappings.explanation: HTTP downloads of executable or script content from external hosts can indicate ingress tool transfer.

evidence_conditions: FTP RETR command downloads an executable or script
Transfer succeeds with reply code 226
File is larger than 10 KB
Transfer is from an external FTP server

external_context.notes: Network location requires network boundary context.

mappings.false_positive_notes: Legitimate FTP software and data transfers may produce similar events.
mappings.explanation: FTP RETR commands downloading executable or script files from external servers provide evidence of ingress tool transfer.
